name: Dropout PI threshold
headline: 4+ / 24h
description: Four or more unexpected dropouts on a single service in 24 hours is a Performance Incident: nbn is expected to investigate, ticket, and if needed roll a truck. Introduced Feb 2022 for HFC, aligned with the existing FTTN metric. Quote it with timestamps when support waves off 'a few drops a day'.

name: Sync caps by tier
headline: tier + ~10%
description: nbn caps FTTN/B sync a little above the tier so overheads still leave full speed at layer 3: 100/40 caps near 110/44, 50/20 near 55/22, 25/10 near 27/11. Sync at the cap means the plan is fully available on the copper; a speed complaint on such a line is a premises/CPE problem, not a line problem.

name: Noise margin floor
headline: 6 dB
description: The standard profile target. Margin far above target with sync at cap is headroom (excellent). At or under 6 dB and falling predicts dropouts before the stability flag catches up. Day vs night swings point at noise ingress (REIN, crosstalk). A 9/12 dB target in the profile string means DLM has already intervened.

name: Co-existence floors
headline: 12/1 Mbps
description: All nbn commits to on FTTN during co-existence (25/5 on FTTB; 25/5 objective after co-existence ends, aligning with the statutory 25 Mbps peak). This is the 'spec' inside 'it's within spec'. Plan-tier shortfalls are remedied through the RSP under ACCC speed-claims guidance (tier move with refund), not through an nbn fault.

name: HFC flap heuristic
headline: 5+ flaps / 24h
description: Take an NTD status reading, wait 24 hours, take another. Five or more new flaps between readings is instability evidence worth a fault, and it sits alongside the 4+/24h Performance Incident threshold. Check in-premises coax (fly lead, wall plate, old pay TV splitters) while the counter runs.

name: Line State
description: Snapshot of the DSLAM port as the node sees the line: sync, attainable, noise margins, attenuation, profile string, stability flag. The modem must be in sync for results to mean anything. The one test that argues with 'it's fine': attainable vs tier and margin vs target settle most speed disputes.

name: Loopback
description: Sends test data both directions between the RSP/nbn side and the premises equipment. Pass proves the layer 2 path worked at that moment, nothing more: it does not measure speed or catch intermittent faults, so it never closes a dropout investigation. Fail while the port shows in sync: power cycle both ends, rerun, escalate.

name: Stability Profile
description: Applies a more conservative DSL profile (higher target margin, interleaving/G.INP) trading speed for holding sync. The standard workflow nbn expects before an instability fault: apply, hold 48 hours, rerun Line State, escalate only if still not STABLE.

name: NTD Status + flaps
description: Operational check on the HFC connection box, with the flap counter as the health signal. Fail: confirm power, reset, retest after 10 minutes, then escalate. RF levels and segment noise are nbn-side only; your leverage is the flap/dropout evidence trail.

name: DPU / DPU Port Status
description: The FTTC pit unit is reverse powered by the NCD over the copper pair: DPU offline means check the NCD's power first, not the internet. DPU Port Status also shows the lead-in sync rate, which should sit near the tier maximum on such short copper; a low rate there is escalation-worthy.

name: UNI-D Status
description: Checks the provisioned Ethernet port on the FTTP NTD and shows the connected MAC. No MAC across two different routers: port or provisioning fault, escalate. Remember only the provisioned UNI-D of the four is live. If MAC shows and loopback passes, the access line is almost never the speed problem.

name: Instability escalation
copy_text: Line State shows the service as UNSTABLE with [N] resyncs. Please apply a stability profile; I will retest in 48 hours and want an nbn instability fault raised if it has not returned to STABLE.
description: Use when the stability flag is anything other than STABLE. Sets up the 48 hour retest so the next call is an escalation, not a repeat.

name: PI dropout escalation
copy_text: I have logged [N] dropouts in 24 hours with timestamps, which exceeds nbn's Performance Incident threshold of 4 unexpected dropouts per day. Please raise it with nbn as a Performance Incident.
description: Use when the dropout diary clears the PI threshold. The timestamps are the evidence; the threshold is the obligation.

name: Speed review (ACCC)
copy_text: Attainable is [X/Y] on a [tier] service. The line cannot support the tier, so please run the speed review process: I want the ACCC remedy options (tier move with refund), and an nbn investigation only if this is a degradation from previous attainable figures.
description: Use when attainable sits below the plan tier. This is a commercial remedy through the RSP, not an nbn fault, and asking for the right process is what makes it move.

name: Degradation with baseline
copy_text: Attainable was [A/B] on [date] (screenshot attached) and is now [C/D] on the same profile. That is a physical degradation of the line, please lodge it with nbn.
description: The strongest fault case there is. Only works if you snapshot baselines when services are healthy: at activation, after nbn work, and at every fault.

name: Line State Interpreter
description: Punch in the numbers from a Line State test and get per-field verdicts, meters, and the escalation script pre-filled with your values. The full decoder guide (every field, every technology, spec section, glossary) lives on the same page.

name: NBN Test Decoder
description: The reference behind the cards: field-by-field line state guide, every technology's tests, what 'in spec' means, escalation playbook, glossary, sources.

name: Tracely (classic)
description: The original guided troubleshooting flows, frozen as built. Kept for reference and honesty about where this section came from; the note generator and port reference are being extracted into standalone tools.
